content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Acme Dedicated - incident review (Jan/Feb) + ownership/escalation
Date: Feb 14, 2025
Time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel, Sean Gallagher, Aisha Bello, Irene Choi, Lauren Bishop
Acme: Priya Shah (Director of Engineering), Mark Jensen (SRE Manager), Elena Ruiz (Staff Platform Engineer), Samir Khan (Ops / Incident Manager)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
- Acme reviewed two recent Dedicated incidents with 5xx/timeouts and intermittent streaming disconnects.
- Key pain point: unclear ownership during incidents (capacity vs routing vs edge/gateway), leading to handoffs and vague ETAs.
- Redwood acknowledged current incident labels are inconsistent across Support/SRE/Infra and proposed standardizing incident categories + owner mapping.
- Discussed response expectations: acknowledgement, update cadence, and how Dedicated comms differ from Hosted API.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Incident #1: dedicated pool saturation / autoscaling lag
- Incident #2: elevated 5xx + streaming drop (gateway vs routing vs runtime)
- Ownership and escalation paths
- Remediation targets / comms expectations

Questions (auto-generated)
- When should Acme page Redwood vs wait for Support updates?
- How do you separate “capacity exhaustion” vs “routing overload” vs “gateway streaming”?
- What are realistic mitigation timelines for Sev1 on Dedicated?

---
Transcript

[00:00] Dev Patel: Alright, cool. I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Dev, I’m the support escalation owner on the Redwood side. Goal today is to do the incident review for the two Jan/Feb events on the Dedicated cluster, and then specifically talk about escalation and, uh, ownership—because I heard pretty clearly from Mark last week that it wasn’t obvious who was driving what.

[00:22] Priya Shah: Yep. That’s accurate. We’re not here to point fingers, but in the moment it felt like we were bounced between, like, three different teams. And the updates were… not always consistent.

[00:34] Dev Patel: Totally fair. Sean’s here from SRE, Irene from infra/fleet, Aisha who’s been helping us with the SLA / remediation mapping, and Lauren from product who owns Dedicated commitments. Mark, do you want to start with your timeline?

[00:49] Mark Jensen: Sure. I’ll do the Feb 2nd one first. Roughly 08:10 UTC we start seeing increased latency, then timeouts, then 5xx from your endpoint. We opened the ticket—uh I think it was SUP-1910? or maybe that was the other one.

[01:06] Samir Khan: It was SUP-1910 for the Feb 9 incident. Feb 2 is in the same thread though.

[01:12] Mark Jensen: Right, thanks. So Feb 2, we page, we get an acknowledgement quickly, but then we’re told it’s “capacity,” and then later it’s “routing,” and then later it’s “GPU nodes unhealthy.” It’s basically three different root causes depending on who answers.

[01:31] Elena Ruiz: And to be super concrete: our app is doing streaming chat completions. We saw a bunch of disconnects mid-stream. So from our point of view it’s like, is that gateway? is it the model server? We couldn’t get a straight answer.

[01:46] Dev Patel: Yep. That’s the core issue we want to fix.

[01:50] Sean Gallagher: This is Sean. Before we go deep, one quick framing. When we’re in active response, we’ve historically used pretty free-form labels. Like “capacity” could mean fleet provisioning, autoscaling policy, scheduler saturation, routing overload, even gateway queueing. It’s not ideal. We’re in the middle of standardizing taxonomy so that when we say “capacity exhaustion,” it means a specific thing with a specific owning team.

[02:15] Priya Shah: Great, but until that exists we still need to know what to do in the moment.

[02:21] Dev Patel: Yep. We’ll get you a one-pager after this call. For now, let’s break down incident 1.

[02:28] Irene Choi: Hi, Irene. I pulled the metrics for your dedicated pool in us-east-1. On Feb 2 we did see sustained GPU utilization at like 97-99% and the request queue depth climbing. Autoscaling did add nodes, but it was slower than it should have been because we hit a quota ceiling on one of the underlying node groups.

[02:53] Elena Ruiz: When you say quota, is that like cloud provider GPU quota or your internal quota?

[02:57] Irene Choi: Internal pool quota plus a cloud limit, kind of both. We reserve for Dedicated, but we still have a ceiling per region and per instance type. We had headroom, just not the exact SKU we needed, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods fast enough.

[03:15] Mark Jensen: So that’s “capacity exhaustion” in your world?

[03:19] Irene Choi: It’s “capacity / provisioning lag.” But this is exactly why Sean’s point matters—right now people will just say “capacity.”

[03:27] Sean Gallagher: In the taxonomy we’re rolling out internally, this would be a “Capacity exhaustion / autoscaling” incident, not routing.

[03:35] Priya Shah: Then why did we get told it was routing?

[03:39] Dev Patel: Because in parallel we also had elevated 429 and 503 and someone saw the router queueing. Mina’s team (routing) jumped in and said “router overload,” but that was downstream of the pool saturation.

[03:52] Elena Ruiz: So the router was overloaded because the pool couldn’t serve?

[03:55] Irene Choi: Correct.

[03:58] Mark Jensen: That is helpful. But it took 45 minutes to get to that clarity.

[04:03] Dev Patel: Yeah. We own that.

[04:05] Lauren Bishop: This is Lauren. Also, on Dedicated, the expectation should be that we tell you (1) are you hard down, (2) are you degraded, (3) what we are doing to mitigate. Even if we don’t have the perfect category, we should not be sending conflicting hypotheses.

[04:22] Priya Shah: Exactly. Even “we think it’s capacity, we’re confirming” is fine. But we got “it’s routing, we’re rolling back” and then later “it’s not routing.”

[04:32] Sean Gallagher: Yep.

[04:34] Aisha Bello: If I can add—Aisha here—part of what we’re implementing is a remediation target by severity and category, and a comms cadence tied to that. So even if the category changes after the fact, the first 15 minutes should have the minimum fields: severity, impacted surface, and an owner.

[04:54] Mark Jensen: Impacted surface meaning… Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?

[04:58] Aisha Bello: Exactly. And within Dedicated, whether it’s gateway, routing/control plane, runtime, fleet. We’re trying to keep it simple.

[05:07] Elena Ruiz: Please keep it simple.

[05:10] Dev Patel: Duly noted.

[05:12] Samir Khan: Can we talk about the Feb 9 one? That’s the one that hurt us more.

[05:16] Dev Patel: Yep, let’s do it.

[05:18] (crosstalk)

[05:20] Mark Jensen: Feb 9 around 17:40 UTC. We see 5xx spikes and a lot of “stream closed” errors on the client side. Our users were mid-conversation, then boom, the stream drops. We had to fail over to our backup provider—OpenAI—temporarily.

[05:38] Priya Shah: And that triggered customer escalations on our side.

[05:41] Dev Patel: Understood.

[05:43] Elena Ruiz: The confusion was: Support told us “we’re seeing gateway issues,” but then SRE told us “runtime nodes are restarting,” and then someone else said “it’s a bad model build.”

[05:56] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. I reviewed the internal post-incident notes. There were two overlapping things: (1) a gateway streaming connection handling regression that increased disconnects under load, and (2) restarts on a subset of inference workers due to a driver issue. The driver restarts were noisy but not the primary customer symptom.

[06:19] Mark Jensen: That seems like something you should decide early—what’s the primary incident.

[06:24] Sean Gallagher: Agree. During the incident, folks were updating based on what they personally were investigating. Without a single category and an owning responder, you get mixed messaging.

[06:36] Dev Patel: This is exactly the incident that drove us to push the taxonomy project faster. We need one “primary incident type” and optional contributing factors.

[06:47] Priya Shah: You keep saying taxonomy—are you going to actually change the process, or just rename labels in Jira?

[06:54] Dev Patel: Change the process. Specifically: in the incident declaration bot (Slack), category will be required, and it will auto-suggest an owner team based on category plus impacted service. If the category is “Edge/Gateway streaming,” the on-call route is different than “Fleet autoscaling.”

[07:13] Elena Ruiz: Is that live?

[07:15] Dev Patel: Not yet for everyone. We’re rolling it out in the next few weeks internally. For you, we can start using it immediately on our side, even if it’s manual.

[07:27] Samir Khan: What about if the category is wrong?

[07:30] Sean Gallagher: Great question. Rule is: pick the best one you can in the first 10-15 minutes. Then we can reclassify after mitigation if needed, but we keep the owning team and comms consistent.

[07:44] Mark Jensen: Ok. On Feb 9, what would the category have been?

[07:49] Sean Gallagher: Primary: “Edge/Gateway - streaming degradation.” Contributing factor: “Runtime worker instability (node restarts).”

[08:00] Elena Ruiz: That’s the first time we’ve heard it phrased that cleanly.

[08:03] Dev Patel: Noted.

[08:05] Priya Shah: Also, can we talk about ETAs? We got, like, “we’re working on it,” for an hour. I need at least a range.

[08:14] Aisha Bello: So, for Sev1, our internal targets are moving toward time-to-mitigate under 30 minutes for the most common categories, but it depends. For a gateway rollback, mitigation can be 15-30 minutes if it’s behind a flag. For capacity provisioning, mitigation might be longer if we have to re-balance nodes across pools.

[08:37] Priya Shah: But you didn’t tell us any of that.

[08:39] Dev Patel: Right. We’re going to align support playbooks so the first update includes: “what we think it is,” “what mitigation path we’re trying,” “next update in X minutes.”

[08:52] Lauren Bishop: And for Dedicated customers we should treat comms as higher-touch. Even if the incident is only affecting one tenant—like you—we should give the same structured updates.

[09:03] Elena Ruiz: Ok.

[09:04] Mark Jensen: One more thing. When we escalated, we weren’t sure whether to page your SRE on-call or just keep replying to the ticket.

[09:11] Dev Patel: That’s on us. Historically we’ve said “use Support,” but for Dedicated Sev1 we want a clear path. We’ll send you a matrix: if it’s Sev1 user-impacting, open the ticket AND page the Dedicated on-call alias. You should not have to guess.

[09:29] Samir Khan: Is that a phone number or Slack?

[09:32] Dev Patel: For you it’ll be email-to-pager plus a Slack connect channel we can set up. (We already have #acme-redwood-support, but we can add the on-call bot there.)

[09:44] Priya Shah: Great.

[09:46] Elena Ruiz: Can I ask a technical question on the streaming disconnects? We saw disconnects even when latency wasn’t that high. That makes me think it’s not just load shedding.

[09:58] Sean Gallagher: Yeah. It wasn’t purely load. There was a regression in the gateway’s streaming heartbeat / keepalive handling. Under certain packet loss patterns, it would close the stream prematurely. Victor’s team (networking) also looked at this, but again, the *primary* was the gateway behavior.

[10:20] Elena Ruiz: Got it. And is that patched?

[10:23] Sean Gallagher: We rolled back the gateway build that introduced it. Permanent fix is in progress; we’re adding a canary plus better metrics on stream resets.

[10:33] Mark Jensen: What’s the timeline on “permanent fix”?

[10:38] Sean Gallagher: I don’t want to over-promise. I can commit to sharing an ETA after we confirm test results. I’d guess 1-2 weeks, but I’m not the code owner for gateway.

[10:51] Dev Patel: And this is where ownership mapping helps. With a category, we know which team owns the permanent fix, and we can track it as an action item with a due date.

[11:01] Priya Shah: Ok, but we also need to understand what you consider Sev1 vs Sev2. We labeled this Sev1 because we had major customer impact.

[11:10] Aisha Bello: We align severity primarily on customer impact and scope. If it’s your production down or materially degraded, it’s Sev1 for Dedicated even if it’s one tenant—because Dedicated is designed for isolation. In the tooling we’ll keep severity definitions stable; taxonomy is separate.

[11:29] Priya Shah: That sounds right.

[11:31] Dev Patel: Can we rewind to the “ownership confusion” moment? Mark, do you remember who you heard from first?

[11:38] Mark Jensen: First response was Support. Then we got a Slack message from someone—maybe SRE?—saying they’re investigating routing. Then another person says “infra has eyes on it.” And we just didn’t know who is incident commander.

[11:54] Samir Khan: We were basically doing triage ourselves from your messages.

[11:58] Sean Gallagher: Yep. Internally we *did* have an IC, but we didn’t clearly identify that person in external comms. That’s a process gap.

[12:08] Dev Patel: For enterprise incidents we should explicitly say: “IC is X, comms owner is Y.” Usually comms owner is Support/CS and IC is SRE/Eng.

[12:20] Priya Shah: Please.

[12:22] Elena Ruiz: And if the incident shifts category, the comms owner shouldn’t change, right?

[12:27] Dev Patel: Exactly.

[12:29] Lauren Bishop: That’s our plan.

[12:31] ---

[12:33] (brief pause)

[12:35] Dev Patel: I want to sanity check: are there any other incidents we should include today?

[12:40] Mark Jensen: Those are the main ones. But we have smaller “brownouts” where latency increases 2-3x and then recovers. Those didn’t trigger pages, but they scare us.

[12:53] Irene Choi: Some of those are from batch jobs on shared underlying hardware, even though it’s Dedicated at the pool level. We’re working on stronger isolation and better headroom.

[13:05] Elena Ruiz: Wait—Dedicated isn’t fully isolated?

[13:08] Irene Choi: Your GPU pool is dedicated. The control plane and gateway are shared components. So you can still be affected by gateway issues that impact multiple customers. But your inference workers are isolated.

[13:22] Priya Shah: That’s important context. We assumed end-to-end was isolated.

[13:27] Lauren Bishop: Thanks for calling that out. We should clarify that in our docs and in the support expectations.

[13:33] Dev Patel: Agreed.

[13:35] Mark Jensen: This gets back to the comms. If gateway is shared, and you have a shared incident, we need to know if we’re the only ones impacted or it’s global.

[13:46] Sean Gallagher: Totally. That’s another metadata field we’re standardizing: “scope” and “customer tier.”

[13:54] Elena Ruiz: Tier meaning like enterprise vs self-serve?

[13:57] Sean Gallagher: Right.

[14:00] Dev Patel: Let’s talk about what you’d like to see during an active incident. If we could design the perfect update template, what’s in it?

[14:09] Priya Shah: Four things: what’s broken, what you think it is, what you’re doing, when you’ll update next. And if you can, a rough ETA range.

[14:20] Mark Jensen: And who is owning it. Like “Infra on-call” vs “Platform” is fine; a name is even better.

[14:27] Elena Ruiz: And whether we should fail over. Like, should we switch traffic away or wait 10 minutes.

[14:33] Dev Patel: That last one is tricky but we can provide guidance, like “we expect mitigation in 15 minutes, otherwise consider failover.”

[14:41] Aisha Bello: Yeah. And we can tie that to severity and category. For instance, capacity provisioning issues might take longer; gateway rollback might be faster.

[14:53] Priya Shah: Great.

[14:55] ---

[15:02] Dev Patel: I’ll share our internal plan at a high level. We’re implementing an incident taxonomy with a small number of top-level categories: capacity/autoscaling, routing/control plane, edge/gateway, runtime/scheduler, model-specific issues, and “external dependency” like cloud provider. Each category has a mapped owning team.

[15:24] Mark Jensen: How many categories total?

[15:26] Dev Patel: We’re targeting ~10 top-level, with optional subtypes. We don’t want 40.

[15:32] Elena Ruiz: Thank you.

[15:34] Priya Shah: And you’re committing to using those in comms to us?

[15:38] Dev Patel: Yes. Even if you don’t see the internal tooling, you’ll see consistent language.

[15:44] Sean Gallagher: And it will reduce internal handoffs too. Paging ambiguity is real—right now people aren’t sure if “capacity” means fleet or routing.

[15:54] Mark Jensen: That is literally what we experienced.

[15:57] ---

[16:01] Samir Khan: Can I ask—when we escalated Feb 9, we got an update that said “we’re talking to runtime.” That made it sound like the runtime team owned it. But you’re saying gateway.

[16:12] Sean Gallagher: Right. There were runtime restarts that were a red herring. Not fully irrelevant, but not primary. We shouldn’t have led with that.

[16:21] Dev Patel: And the comms owner should have consolidated, not forwarded raw internal notes.

[16:28] Priya Shah: Yeah, it felt like we were reading your Slack.

[16:31] Dev Patel: That’s a good way to put it.

[16:34] ---

[16:38] Elena Ruiz: While we have Irene: do we have enough capacity headroom? We have a launch end of March.

[16:46] Irene Choi: We should review your forecast. Right now you’re peaking around X tokens/sec—sorry, I don’t want to say the exact number on a recorded call, but we can follow up in email. We can set a target headroom percentage and ensure autoscaling can reach it within minutes.

[17:06] Mark Jensen: We can share forecast ranges.

[17:09] Irene Choi: Great.

[17:11] Lauren Bishop: And if you need reserved burst capacity for that launch, we can talk about it. Dedicated contracts can include temporary burst.

[17:20] Priya Shah: Ok, we’ll take that offline.

[17:23] ---

[17:25] Dev Patel: Quick check—do you have any compliance/security folks that need to understand incident handling? Sometimes procurement asks for response timelines.

[17:33] Priya Shah: We have security, but this is more operational. Though our procurement team did ask why we failed over to OpenAI. They’re evaluating Bedrock too. So yes, we’ll eventually need a crisp statement of your incident response and escalation.

[17:49] Dev Patel: Understood. We have a security review call template too, but for today we’ll keep it on reliability.

[17:56] ---

[18:00] Dev Patel: I’m going to propose concrete deliverables from Redwood.

[18:04] Dev Patel: One: escalation and ownership map for Dedicated, including what to page for Sev1.

[18:09] Dev Patel: Two: comms template—first update within 10 minutes, then every 30 minutes for Sev1 unless we agree otherwise.

[18:17] Dev Patel: Three: for the Feb 9 incident specifically, we’ll provide a written summary: primary category, contributing factors, mitigations taken, and the permanent fix tracking.

[18:28] Mark Jensen: That would help. We had to write our own internal postmortem and it was missing key details.

[18:35] Sean Gallagher: And to be clear, we’ll still do a full internal postmortem, but we can share the customer-safe version.

[18:42] Priya Shah: Please do.

[18:44] ---

[18:47] (noise, someone typing)

[18:50] Elena Ruiz: Can I confirm terminology? You said “edge/gateway streaming.” Is that the same as your API gateway? Or is it, like, Envoy?

[18:58] Sean Gallagher: It’s our edge tier in front of the inference service, including streaming handling. It’s similar to a gateway / reverse proxy plus some Redwood-specific logic for streaming and auth.

[19:10] Elena Ruiz: Ok.

[19:12] Mark Jensen: And “routing” is the smart routing layer? Like model selection?

[19:16] Sean Gallagher: Exactly—policy, region selection, fallback, and queueing.

[19:22] Mark Jensen: Helpful.

[19:24] ---

[19:26] Priya Shah: One last complaint. During Feb 2, we got asked multiple times for the same logs. That’s also a sign of handoffs.

[19:35] Dev Patel: Yeah. Another thing we’re adding is a minimum incident intake checklist so we don’t re-ask. Also, if category + owner is set, there’s less “ping-pong.”

[19:48] Samir Khan: Great.

[19:50] ---

[19:52] Dev Patel: I think that covers the meat. Anything else you want from us?

[19:57] Mark Jensen: Just consistency. If you say it’s capacity, it should mean capacity. If you say it’s routing, it should mean routing. And tell us who owns it.

[20:07] Elena Ruiz: And streaming disconnects—we need confidence that’s resolved before end of March.

[20:14] Sean Gallagher: Understood.

[20:16] Irene Choi: Same.

[20:18] ---

[20:20] Dev Patel: Alright, recap and next steps.

[20:23] Dev Patel: I’ll send the escalation map by Tuesday.

[20:26] Dev Patel: Aisha will send a customer-facing summary of remediation targets / response expectations.

[20:32] Dev Patel: Irene will propose capacity headroom / autoscaling adjustments and we’ll schedule a short follow-up with Elena and Mark.

[20:40] Dev Patel: And Sean will coordinate on the Feb 9 customer-safe writeup with the owning engineering team.

[20:47] Priya Shah: Sounds good.

[20:49] Mark Jensen: Thanks everyone.

[20:51] Dev Patel: Thank you. We’ll follow up in the ticket thread and email.

---
End of transcript
